slides.say: Now remainders. A remainder is what's left when we divide one number by another. Ten divided by three. Three fits into ten three times, up to nine, and one is left. So the remainder is one.

Another example, fifty-three divided by seven. Seven sevens are forty-nine, and fifty-three minus forty-nine is four. So the remainder is four. The number we divide by, seven, is the divisor, and how many whole times it fits, here also seven, is the quotient. So fifty-three is seven times seven, plus four.
at: So fifty-three is seven times seven

slides.say: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor. If seven or more were left, the seven would fit one more time.
Here's where students usually go wrong. What's the remainder when we divide five by eight? It's five, not three. The remainder is not the difference between the numbers.
at: What's the remainder when we divide five

slides.say: Think of a shop. Each drink costs eight shekels, and you have thirty-five shekels. You buy as many as you can: eight, sixteen, twenty-four, thirty-two. That's four drinks, and three shekels stay in your hand. Three is the remainder.

Now you walk in with only five shekels. That's not enough for even one drink. You get zero drinks, and the five shekels stay in your hand. So five divided by eight is zero, with a remainder of five. The remainder is what's left in your hand after you buy as many as you can.

What remainders can we get when we divide by four? Let's try. One divided by four leaves one. Two leaves two, and three leaves three. Four divides exactly, so it leaves zero. Five leaves one again, and six leaves two.
at: One divided by four leaves one

slides: So the remainders go round and round: one, two, three, zero. The biggest remainder is three, one less than four. With one more, the four would fit again.

slides.say: That's a rule: the biggest remainder is always one less than the divisor. Dividing by ten, the biggest remainder is nine. Dividing by twelve, it's eleven.
The digit sum gives us one more gift, but only for three and nine. Five thousand four hundred thirty-two has a digit sum of five plus four plus three plus two, which is fourteen.
at: has a digit sum of five plus four

slides.say: Fourteen divided by nine leaves five, so five thousand four hundred thirty-two divided by nine also leaves five. And fourteen divided by three leaves two, so the big number divided by three leaves two as well.
at: Fourteen divided by nine leaves five

slides.say: Another example, two hundred twenty. Its digit sum is two plus two plus zero, which is four. Four divided by three leaves one, so two hundred twenty divided by three leaves one. This works only for three and nine. For four or seven, the digit sum tells us nothing about the remainder. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
